In Keritot, however, the discussion concerns whether annulment remains possible at the present stage, and after slaughter it does not. The sugyot therefore speak from different perspectives. Regarding a rented courtyard, siman 313 states that a courtyard rented to another may nevertheless acquire for the landlord, even though it is in the tenant's possession. Sema asks from siman 260, seif 4, where if landlord and tenant live together and a disabled deer enters, both can acquire it. In my view the distinction is as follows. Although a person's courtyard can acquire for him without his awareness, a rented courtyard acquires for the tenant only when the tenant consciously wants the courtyard to acquire, such as where the transferor intends to transfer through the rented courtyard. But when a lost object enters without the tenant's awareness, it belongs to the owner of the courtyard. A rented courtyard is certainly also the tenant's hand. Ran explains that a courtyard is like a hand because a person ordinarily places everything beneficial to him there. The same is true of a rented courtyard. But the underlying corpus remains the landlord's, and it is also his hand in a basic sense. The tenant has rented the owner's "hand" for the purposes of the rental. This resembles a hired worker. Siman 270 says a worker's own found object belongs to him because the employer did not hire him for that purpose. Likewise, a minor daughter's ordinary found object belongs to her father because her hand is treated as his. Even if another person hired the daughter for work, an unrelated found object can still belong according to the underlying family rule because she was not hired for finding. So too with a rented courtyard: when a lost object enters without the tenant's awareness, the rental was not made for that acquisition, and the landlord remains the one whose courtyard receives the found object. But siman 260 speaks of a disabled deer or fledglings that cannot fly, where Sema in siman 268, seif katan 15, requires the claimant to say, "My field shall acquire for me." Siman 270 says that if one hires a worker for all tasks and then specifically points out found objects for him to gather, the finds belong to the employer. The worker's hand is then being used for the hired purpose. Similarly, if the tenant sees the found object entering and says, "My field shall acquire it for me," he is using the rented courtyard for the very purpose covered by his possession, like directing a worker to gather found objects. The find therefore belongs to the tenant. This also answers Raavad's question on Rambam from the incident in Bava Metzia where a place was rented in order to acquire produce. It also explains our ruling in siman 198 that if the seller's house is rented to the buyer and the object is there, the buyer acquires through courtyard even though siman 313 says a rented courtyard can acquire for the landlord. When the tenant-buyer expressly wants the rented space to acquire the purchased object, the rental is being used for that purpose and it is his courtyard for that object. Conversely, if the buyer's courtyard is rented to the seller and the seller's merchandise remains there, the buyer-landlord does not acquire merely because the goods rest in the corpus of his land. As against ordinary goods the rented space is the tenant-seller's domain. Only with an unrelated found object, which the tenant never intended the rental to cover, do we revert to the landlord's residual courtyard right. MahariT, responsum 65, writes that the landlord acquires even merchandise resting in a courtyard rented to the seller, treating it as the landlord's courtyard. In my view the ruling in siman 195 points the other way, because when the buyer's courtyard is rented to the seller, acquisition there is treated as dependent on money rather than as courtyard acquisition. I later saw Machaneh Efrayim, who likewise disagrees with MahariT, though for a different reason. He says every acquisition requires movement from one domain to another. When the seller has rented the place, the object has not yet left his domain; when the seller rents the location of the goods to the buyer, the site itself has partially passed to the buyer and the goods therefore move with it. My explanation above remains, in my view, the primary rationale. And a courtyard that is borrowed rather than rented is the same. Borrowing and renting both create possessory use rights. Eruvin 30, Tosafot, implies that a borrowed courtyard can acquire for the borrower. A worker is different: to acquire the legal status of a hired servant one ordinarily needs payment, because an unpaid worker can withdraw even from work involving potential loss, as explained in siman 333. A courtyard, however, is not a servant; the borrower receives a property-use right. The tenant can also acquire for a third person through his rented courtyard, because for covered uses the courtyard is fully his. Only with a found object arriving without his awareness does the landlord acquire, because that was not part of the rental purpose. Concerning a deposited object that the depositor later transfers to the custodian, Taz in siman 189 writes that the custodian does not acquire through his own courtyard because Rashbam says the custodian's premises where the deposit rests are treated as the depositor's domain. MahariT rejects this for several reasons. First, by what kinyan did the depositor acquire the custodian's space? Renting land ordinarily requires money or chazakah. Second, if no specific place was designated, no defined area was ever transferred to the depositor. Third, when the depositor now transfers the deposit to the custodian, the custodian's courtyard and the gift can become effective together. MahariT is correct. Ketzot HaChoshen attempts to reject the proofs, but in my view his objections do not stand. Permission for use alone does not create the kind of land right needed to make the place an acquiring courtyard, as I wrote in siman 192. Even if the depositor had permission to place the object wherever convenient, the custodian remains entitled to move it from place to place, so no particular spot ceases to be the custodian's courtyard. And the depositor can certainly waive any residual claim against the custodian and allow the custodian to hold the object in his own house merely by speech; no additional proof is needed. Ketzot himself cites a clear proof for MahariT from Kiddushin 47: if a man betroths a woman with a deposit of his that is already in her house, she is betrothed. That is decisive. For partners acquiring from one another through a shared courtyard, see what I wrote at the beginning of siman 176. Practical rules emerging from the introduction
A person's courtyard that is unguarded, while he stands beside it, works according to everyone through the law of hand because it resembles one's nearby hand. This applies to an adult. A male minor does not have that type of hand, because an adult sleeping beside the courtyard also fails where awareness and guarding are required. A minor, who lacks that awareness, is like a sleeping person. A female minor is different because Scripture specifically treats her courtyard beside her as hand for gittin, and that rule can extend to monetary law. Because an adult's nearby courtyard works as hand, a non Jew likewise acquires through an unguarded courtyard when standing beside it. A non Jew has a hand and has awareness to guard; he is unlike a minor. A guarded courtyard where the owner does not stand beside it works, according to Rif and Rosh, through agency. Therefore a male minor, female minor, and non Jew do not acquire in that manner because they lack ordinary agency. Shach in siman 243 disagrees and says a female minor can acquire monetary property through such a guarded courtyard without standing beside it, but the primary ruling follows the majority of authorities. According to Ran, an adult's guarded courtyard can work as hand even without standing beside it, because anything beneficial to him is normally placed there and the courtyard is like an extended hand. According to Ran, a non Jew can therefore acquire through a guarded courtyard without standing beside it as well. However, Ran's reasoning does not apply to male or female minors, because they are not people who legally maintain guarded courtyards in that sense. Property in their hands can itself be treated as knowingly exposed to loss, and they also lack agency. Thus even Ran agrees that minors do not acquire through a guarded courtyard unless they stand beside it where the special female-minor rule can operate. A guarded courtyard acquires for an adult even while he sleeps, because the courtyard guards itself. An unguarded courtyard, which requires standing beside it, does not acquire while he sleeps. An unguarded courtyard where the person does not stand beside it does not acquire at all according to Rif and Rambam, even for a gift, because they do not rule like Rav Pappa in Bava Metzia 11. Rosh and Ran, who do rule like Rav Pappa, hold that a gift can be acquired there through agency when another person consciously transfers it. Therefore minors and non Jews, who lack agency, do not acquire even a gift in that manner. The general rule that a courtyard can acquire without the owner's awareness operates in such cases only through agency; minors and non Jews therefore do not receive that advantage. A courtyard of hekdesh does not acquire an ordinary lost sum of money even according to Ramban, who recognizes a form of hand for hekdesh, because the treasurer's status itself is agency of Heaven and ordinary agency cannot acquire a found object where others are prejudiced and there is no appointment by the property's owner. But if one consecrates a cistern and it fills with water, or a dovecote and it fills with doves, the courtyard can acquire because no one else is prejudiced by property that would not have arisen there absent the hekdesh structure, and true ownerless property has no owner from whom agency is required. Likewise, if a person gives a gift to hekdesh and places it in a hekdesh courtyard, hekdesh acquires because there is another person's conscious transfer and no prejudice to others. A private person may also acquire ownerless property for hekdesh through his own courtyard where he could have acquired it for himself. Sacred property delivered to the treasurer can no longer be annulled, because delivery to the treasurer functions like meshichah. A courtyard rented or borrowed through a valid kinyan is the courtyard and hand of the tenant or borrower. It resembles hiring the owner's hand for the agreed use. An unrelated found object entering without the tenant's awareness ordinarily belongs to the landlord because the courtyard was not rented for that purpose. But if the tenant sees the find and says that his rented field should acquire it, it belongs to the tenant, like a worker expressly directed to gather finds. All the more so, a gift placed there for the tenant is acquired by the tenant, even if the landlord himself is the donor. The tenant may also acquire for another through the rented courtyard. Conversely, where the tenant gives a gift to the landlord while it remains in the rented courtyard, the landlord does not acquire merely by virtue of ownership of the underlying land, because for ordinary uses the courtyard is presently the tenant's domain. The general principle is that a rented or borrowed courtyard functions like the hand of the tenant or borrower for the purposes included within his possessory use. Concerning the opinion that a courtyard guarded by the seller is sufficient, Shach, seif katan 1, asks from Kiddushin 27. There the Gemara explains Rabban Gamliel's transfer as acquisition by agav. If Rav Pappa's rule of another transferring mind were accepted, why not say the acquisition occurred through courtyard? In my view, the Gemara needed agav because of the poor man's tithe transferred through R. Akiva for the poor. Even if the tithe given directly to R. Yehoshua could be acquired through the rented courtyard, R. Akiva could not acquire for the poor merely through his courtyard unless after the donor's statement R. Akiva himself expressly caused his courtyard to acquire for them. The Mishnah does not record such a statement. Therefore that transfer must have worked through agav. The Gemara's proof in Kiddushin is thus from the poor man's tithe, not necessarily from the tithe delivered personally to R. Yehoshua. The latter could work through courtyard even though agav would be difficult because the donor's discretionary benefit in choosing the recipient is not treated as property. The grain in the incident was still tevel, as Shitah Mekubetzet explains, and Rabban Gamliel transferred whatever tithe he would later separate. Regarding terumat ma'aser, the remaining interest is only the discretionary benefit of choosing the recipient, and that is not property sufficient for agav. Nor can we treat the tevel as ordinary property because use involving destruction is prohibited while it remains tevel for terumah and terumat ma'aser. Poor man's tithe differs. Destructive benefit from produce that is tevel only to poor man's tithe is permitted; the special terumah prohibition does not apply. Such produce therefore has ordinary monetary value through fuel and similar uses, and can be transferred through agav. This is the source of the Gemara's proof. R. Yehoshua's terumat ma'aser, by contrast, could require Rav Pappa's courtyard rationale.
Nevertheless, if the seller... See Shach, seif katan 2, who questions this clause. According to the opinion that another person's conscious transfer allows acquisition through a courtyard guarded by the seller, the buyer should acquire even here, as the sugya in Bava Metzia implies. Taz also asks why the text says "the courtyard itself" and what that phrase excludes. In my view the words "Nevertheless, if the seller..." do not belong here. They should appear at the beginning of the gloss, referring back to Mechaber's statement that a guarded courtyard acquires. Rama means that if the seller rented to the buyer the very courtyard that is itself guarded by the seller, while the seller's other goods remain mixed in it, and the buyer merely rented the place occupied by the goods he bought, the place is treated as unguarded relative to the buyer and does not acquire for him. This also explains the phrase "the courtyard itself." It is specifically where the seller rented the same courtyard to the buyer while the seller's own goods remained intermixed. But if the seller's goods were located in the buyer's own courtyard and the seller sold only some of them, the courtyard remains guarded for the buyer even though the seller retains a right of entry to reach his remaining goods. The seller is then like a guest whose access does not destroy the buyer's guarding control. Accordingly, when the transferor himself guards the goods and the buyer has a genuine rented possessory space, the opinion that another transferring mind suffices can still apply. But where the goods are entirely in a truly unguarded courtyard of the buyer, even sale or gift does not help merely because the donor is present. The reason that sale can help in some unguarded settings is that the transferor's guarding is treated as the recipient's guarding. Yet even the recipient's own guarding from outside an unguarded courtyard is insufficient unless he stands in the required position so that the courtyard resembles his hand. The transferor's guarding cannot be stronger than the recipient's own guarding. This also refutes Shitah Mekubetzet's suggestion that a gift is always considered to be in a guarded courtyard because no one else is permitted to take it. Our ruling requires the courtyard to resemble the recipient's hand or agent in the legally prescribed manner; mere legal protection from strangers is not enough. Even though Beit Yosef writes that an unguarded courtyard, guarded neither by seller nor buyer, does not acquire, there is a further application. Suppose Reuven gave movable property to Shimon and rented him the place where the goods lay, while the goods remained mixed with Reuven's property. According to the opinion that guarding by the transferor is sufficient, Shimon acquires. Later Shimon transfers those same goods to Levi and also assigns Levi the possessory right he had in Reuven's courtyard for keeping them. Levi can acquire even though the courtyard is not guarded by Shimon, his transferor, or by Levi himself. It is sufficient that it remains guarded by Reuven, the transferor from Shimon's own transferor. Proof appears from the Mishnah where Rabban Gamliel gave tithe to R. Yehoshua and rented him its place. R. Yehoshua then stood and gave terumat ma'aser to R. Elazar ben Azaryah and rented its place to him. The courtyard was not guarded by R. Yehoshua or R. Elazar ben Azaryah; it remained guarded by Rabban Gamliel, the previous transferor. Yet the acquisition could work according to the same theory. Thus guarding by the transferor's transferor can suffice where the chain of possessory rights is established.
It is so hard that the courtyard is so hard that it is so near that the courtyard is guarded by it, and it seems that the courtyard is not preserved, and that it is not the case that the court itself is not like a messenger, and that it is not like a messenger, and that it is not the same as the one who is not known There is not only a hundred of her mother and can be repaired, but certainly, a hand-to-dresser, and a place in it, even if the field is large, and the other side that is not preserved in his name is not the case of Hashem’s name, nor does he say that he is not called a buffer, and that he is not called a buffer, and that he is not called a s “As a vessel in the memorial, my mother bought Dea Lao and stood in it, it is not possible in the vessel, but by the hands of the vessel as the court and sat down in the preserved courtyard:
A person's four cubits. See Shach, seif katan 5, who discusses why the Sages still needed to institute meshichah in a side alley if four cubits already acquire there. In my view the answer is simple. Meshichah is needed where the seller is also standing there. In that case the buyer certainly does not acquire automatically through four cubits. Meshichah acquires in a side alley even if the seller arrived first and initially occupied those four cubits. Ketzot HaChoshen writes that according to Ran, who distinguishes whether the vessel came first, the place occupied by a vessel in a side alley can become associated with the vessel's owner. He then suggests that kiddushin differs because four cubits were instituted even in the public domain. Therefore, if the husband threw kiddushin into the public domain and afterward the woman entered the surrounding four cubits, she could become betrothed, because the place where the kiddushin rested never became the husband's acquiring domain. In my view this cannot be correct. If so, even if the husband himself first entered those four cubits in the public domain and the woman entered afterward, he should still be able to throw her get or kiddushin there, because the husband has no ordinary acquisition in public-domain four cubits. Yet Gittin 78 says we must examine which one entered the four cubits first. Necessarily the Sages gave the public domain, for purposes of gittin and kiddushin, the same functional law as a side alley to both husband and wife. Just as the husband's prior presence can defeat the woman's four-cubit acquisition there, his vessels or money already resting there can also prevent the place from becoming hers.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he:
המשתמר לדעתו. דהלוקח אבל משומר לדעת המוכר לא מהני דבעינן דומיא דידו שהוא משתמר לדעתו והי"ח ס"ל דבדעת אחרת מקנה שמירת המקנה חשיב כשמירת הקונה (סמ"ע) וע"ב ס"ק ג' דכשהוא מוקף מחיצות אף שאינו נעול במנעול ואף שאינו מקורה מיקרי חצר המשתמרת:
וכן נראה להורות והש"ך כ' דהעיקר כדעת המחבר דהא סתמא דהש"ס בקדושין דף כ"ו מסיק דר"ג הקנה לר"י ע"י חצירו והיה בתורת אגב אלמא דחצר שאינו משתמר אינו קונה אפי' בדעת אחרת מקנה אותו ומ"מ לא רצה להכריע נגד הרב לכן כ' דהוי ספיקא דדינא (וע"ב שיש ליישב קושית הש"ך):
מעורבין לאו דוקא אלא כל שאין הפסק מחיצה ביניהם מקרי חצר שאינו משתמר (סמ"ע) והש"ך והט"ז תמהו על רמ"א דמה בכך דמיקרי חצר שאינו משתמרת הא לדיעה זו קונה אפי' בחצר שאינו משתמרת היכא דאיכא דעת אחרת מקנה אותו ☜ וע"ב דהאי ומיהו אין מקומו כאן וצ"ל קודם היש חולקים וקאי אהמחבר ולכך כתב הרב שהשכיר לו החצר עצמו להורות דדוקא כשהחצר היה של המקנה רק שהשכיר להקונה מקום בפירות ולא היה הפסק המחיצות בין המטלטלין שקנה לשל המוכר אז מקרי אינו משתמר ולא קנה אבל כשהיה החצר של הלוקח ופירות של מוכר מונחים שם ומכר לו מקצת הפירות ולא היה הפסק מחיצה בין הפירות שקנה לפירות של המוכר מיקרי חצר המשתמר וקנה אפי' להמחבר דכל שאין גוף החצר שלו לא הוי רק כאכסנאי שאין מבטל שמירת המקבל:
ויש חולקים לדעה זו קנה אפי' הי' מעורבין בחצרו של המקנה ☜ וע"ב דדוקא בכה"ג פליגי הי"ח אבל בחצר של המקבל ואינו משתמר לגמרי דבעינן עומד בצדו לא מהני מה שהמקנה עומד בצדו ועיין עוד ביאורים דבחצר המשתמר רק שהפירות מעורבין שקנה לדעת הי"ח אם הקונה הזה הקנה הפירות לאחר ע"י חצרו של המקנה שלו קנה אותו האחר כיון שהוא משומר לדעת הנותן של הנותן שלו:
בצד אותו רשות ☜ וע"ב דבעינן דוקא בצדו ממש אפי' להמחבר דבעינן ידו בסמוכה לו אבל בעומד ברחוק קצת ואפי' יכול לשמרו לא מהני ואם עומד בצדו או אפי' בתוכו בעינן ג"כ שיכול לשמרו לפיכך שדה גדולה ומציאה מונחת בתוכה בצד אחר והוא עומד בצד השני לא קנה לפי שאינו יכול לשומרו:
דארבע אמות והר"ן מחלק דדוקא כשקדם המקבל לכלי לתוך הד"א אבל כשקדם הכלי נקנה המקום לבעל הכלי ושוב אין המקבל יכול לקנות בד"א והרבה פוסקים לא חלקו בכך וס"ל דאפי' קדם הכלי קנה (סמ"ע) והא דהוצרכו לתקן משיכה היינו שעומד חוץ לד"א ומושך או שהמשיכה הוא קנין דאורייתא וע"ב דנפקא מינה עוד שהוצרכו לתקן משיכה היכא דהנותן בעצמו בא קודם לתוך הד"א דאז לכ"ע לא קני בד"א ובעי משיכה דוקא ועיין עוד ביאורים דבקדושין דד"א מהני אף ברה"ר מ"מ אם קדם כסף הקדושין ואח"כ באתה האשה לתוך הד"א אינה מקודשת דלענין קידושין נתנו חכמים לרשות הרבים דין סימטא שיהי' לו קנין אף להבעל:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en:
Guarded according to his awareness. Meaning according to the purchaser's awareness. If it is guarded only according to the seller's awareness, it is ineffective, because the purchaser's courtyard must resemble his hand, which is guarded according to his own awareness. The dissenting view holds that when another person intentionally transfers property to him, the transferor's guarding is treated like the recipient's guarding. Sema. See the Beurim, seif katan 3, that if the area is enclosed by walls, even if it is not locked and not roofed, it is considered a guarded courtyard:
And it appears proper to rule this way. The Shach writes that the principal ruling follows the Mechaber, because the plain conclusion of the Gemara in Kiddushin 26 is that Rabban Gamliel transferred property to Rabbi Yehoshua through the latter's courtyard as an agav acquisition. This indicates that an unguarded courtyard does not acquire even where another person intentionally transfers the property. Nevertheless, the Shach did not wish to rule against the Rama and therefore writes that it remains a doubt of law. See the Beurim for a resolution of the Shach's difficulty:
Mixed together. This is not literal. Whenever there is no partition separating the respective property, the courtyard is considered unguarded. Sema. The Shach and Taz question the Rama: what difference does it make that the courtyard is called unguarded, when according to this view it acquires even through an unguarded courtyard where another person intentionally transfers the property? See the Beurim. The clause beginning "however" does not belong here. It should appear before "and some disagree" and refers to the Mechaber. Therefore the Rama speaks of a courtyard that the transferor himself rented to the purchaser, teaching that specifically where the body of the courtyard still belongs to the transferor, who merely rented the purchaser a place for his produce, and there is no partition between the purchaser's acquired goods and the seller's remaining goods, it is considered unguarded and does not acquire. But where the courtyard itself belongs to the purchaser and the seller's produce is lying there, and the seller sells him part of that produce without a partition between the purchased produce and the seller's remaining produce, the courtyard is considered guarded and acquires even according to the Mechaber. A seller's goods in another person's courtyard do not nullify the purchaser's guarding, because anyone whose body of the courtyard is not his is like a guest and does not defeat the resident's control:
And some disagree. According to this view he acquires even if the goods are mixed together in the transferor's own courtyard. See the Beurim. The dissent applies specifically in this type of case. But where the recipient's courtyard is itself completely unguarded, such that he must stand beside it, the transferor's standing there does not help. See further in the Beurim: if the courtyard is fundamentally guarded but the purchased produce is mixed with other produce, then according to the dissenting view, if this purchaser later transfers the produce to a third person by means of the original transferor's courtyard, that third person acquires, because the courtyard is guarded according to the awareness of the current giver, who is the owner of the produce being transferred:
Beside that domain. See the Beurim. He must stand literally beside it, even according to the Mechaber, because we require his hand, as it were, to be adjacent to the courtyard. Standing at some distance is ineffective even if he can watch it. Conversely, even if he stands beside it or within it, he must also be capable of guarding it. Therefore, if a large field contains a found object at one end and he stands at the other end, he does not acquire it because he cannot effectively guard the object from there:
Four cubits. The Ran distinguishes that the recipient acquires through his four cubits only if he entered those four cubits before the utensil. If the utensil entered first, the space is acquired for the owner of the utensil and the recipient cannot afterward acquire through the same four cubits. Many authorities make no such distinction and hold that even if the utensil arrived first, he acquires. Sema. The reason the Sages nevertheless had to enact meshichah is that one may be standing outside the relevant four cubits and then pull the item, or because meshichah may itself be a Torah acquisition. See the Beurim for another practical difference: if the transferor himself entered the four cubits first, all agree the recipient does not acquire through those four cubits and needs meshichah. See further in the Beurim. Although four cubits can effect kiddushin even in the public domain, if the kiddushin money entered first and the woman only afterward entered those four cubits, she is not betrothed. For kiddushin, the Sages gave the public domain the status of a side alley in which the husband may also acquire rights in the space:

siftei_kohen.he:
[" וכן נראה להורות כו'. ונראה שטעם הרב שנמשך אחר מ\"ש הרא\"ש פ\"ק דמציעא וז\"ל ורב אלפס ז\"ל לא הביא דברי רב פפא ומתוך דבריו משמע שאין מחלק בין מציאה למתנה וסבר כשנוי קמא דמטלטלים אג\"ק הקנה להם ויותר נראה כאשר כתבתי דרב פפא בתרא' הוא וגם רב אשי מתקן דבריו מה שהקשה לו רב שימי מגט למתנה עכ\"ל אבל לפע\"ד נראה עיקר כהרי\"ף ורמב\"ם דהכי מוכח כול' סוגיא דסתם ש\"ס פ\"ק דקידושין (דף כ\"ז) דבעי למפשט התם מעובדא דר\"ג דבעי' צבורי' במטלטלי אג\"ק ודחי דילמא התם כי היכא דלא ליטרחינהו ובתר ה\"ק נמי אבעיא להו שדה במכר ומטלטלין במתנה מהו ת\"ש עישור שאני עתיד למוד נתון ליהושע ומקומו מושכר לו ש\"מ והובא כל זה בהרי\"ף והרא\"ש פ\"ק דקידושין ובשאר הפוסקים אלמא דלא ס\"ל לסתם ש\"ס כשנויא דרב פפא דאל\"כ היכא פשוט מהתם דילמא התם לאומדין אג\"ק הוי אלא מטעם חצירו וכשנוי' דרב פפא (הגה ועוד קשה לפע\"ד דאם איתא לדרב פפא ל\"ל לר\"ג לאגב תיפוק ליה דבלא\"ה קנה מטעם חצרו) הגם שאפשר לדחוק וליישב מ\"מ נלפע\"ד עיקר מכח הסוגיא זו דליתי' לשנויי דרב פפא ואין להאריך (ומ\"ש הרא\"ש וגם ר\"א מתרץ דבריו יתבאר לקמן) כ\"כ ה\"ה פ\"ד מה' זכיה וז\"ל ויש פוסקים כרב פפא והרמב\"ן ז\"ל כתב מתוך דברי הרי\"ף ז\"ל נראה שהוא משוה מתנה למציאה וכן מוכחת הסוגיא שבספ\"ק דקידושין וזהו דעת המחבר ז\"ל עכ\"ל ומביאו ב\"י לקמן סי' רמ\"ג סעיף כ\"ה וכ\"כ הריטב\"א פ\"ק דמציעא וז\"ל ואיכא מאן דפסק כרב פפא דבתרא הוא וסוגיין הכא כוותיה וכן דעת הרב ר\"י בר ראובן ברצלוני ומיהו מדברי הרי\"ף נראה דלא ס\"ל הכי אלא אף במתנה בעי עומד בצד שדהו כמו במציאה והפקר דאע\"ג דשני לן משום דעת אחרת מקנה לענין רץ אחריהם לא שני לן בהא והכי ודאי מסתברא דהא בקידושין בפ\"ק נקיט כתירוצא קמא דהכא דהתם בעי לענין אגב מטלטלין במתנה ושדה במכר ופשיט ליה ממעשה דר' גמליאל וזקנים ומדפשיט ליה ש\"ס מיניה אלמא דס\"ל דמדין אגב ולא משום חצר דרב פפא וכיון דהכי הוא מסתברא דליתיה לדרב פפא עכ\"ל וכן משמע עוד להדיא בדברי הריטב\"א להדיא פ\"ק דקידושין ע\"ש בריטב\"א סביב הש\"ס בסוף דף ל\"ד וכ\"כ התוס' רי\"ד פ\"ק דקידושין דף כ\"ז ע\"א דכל זו השיטה אתיא דלא כרב פפא וכן דעת הסמ\"ג דף קס\"א ע\"ד וכן נראה דעת ר\"י נט\"ו ח\"ב וכן נראה דעת הר\"ן שהביא ב\"י לקמן ס\"ס רמ\"ג ומ\"ש הרא\"ש דרב אשי מתרץ דברי רב פפא אינה ראיה לפע\"ד דאפי' יהיה כן דרב אשי ס\"ל כרב פפא מ\"מ כיון דמסתמא דש\"ס פ\"ק דקידושין לא ס\"ל הכי לא קי\"ל הכי ועוד שכבר כתב הב\"י ס\"ס רמ\"ג בשם הר\"ן דרב אשי לאו לפרוקי אליבא דרב פפא לחוד אתא אלא כי היכא דלא תיקשי לדידן גט דאפי' משתמרת בעינן עומדת בצד ביתה כו' עכ\"ל וכ\"כ הריטב\"א פ\"ק דמציעא וברור הוא אך כיון שראיתי שגם בעל העיטור בריש אות קנין ס\"ל כהר\"י ברצולני וכהרא\"ש ומביאו ב\"י לעיל סי' קצ\"ו מחו' ח' וכן דעת ראב\"ן ריש מציעא ריש דף צ\"ד וכ\"כ בהגהות מרדכי פ\"ק דמציעא ובהגהת מיי' פ\"ג ופ\"ה דה' מכירה איני כדאי להכריע והוי ספיקא דדינא אבל להורות לכתחלה וכמ\"ש הרב ודאי לא נהירא שכבר בררתי שדעת רוב הפוסקים כהרי\"ף והרמב\"ם ושכן עיקר:"]
[" מיהו אם המוכר כו' דברי הר\"ב בזה תמוהין דהוציא כן ממ\"ש הב\"י בשם הגהות מרדכי פ\"ק דמציעא ובהגה\"מ שם עצמו מבואר בשם ר\"י דלא כתב כן אלא לתירוצא קמא בש\"ס דצריך חצר המשתמרת אף במכר ומתנה והלכך כיון שאין הפסק בין הפירות והן מעורבין ה\"ל חצר שאינו משתמרת והוא דעת המחבר וסייעתו וא\"כ להרב שפסק כר' פפא קנה אף במעורבין וכן מבואר להדיא בהגהות מרדכי שם וז\"ל אם מקנה אדם לחבירו פירות שהם בביתו ומשכיר לו מקומן ואין הפסק בין אותן פירות לפירות של בע\"ה לא קנה ומיקרי חצר שאינו משתמרת ובמציא' לא קניא להחצר מיהו במתנה מסיק רב פפא דקני משום דדעת אחרת מקנה אותו שאני פי' ר\"י עכ\"ל וכ\"כ בהגהות מיי' פ' ד' דה' מכירה וכן מוכח בתוס' פ\"ק דמציעא סוף דף י\"א ושלא כדברי הר\"ב:"]
[" דוקא בתוכו כו' ל' המ\"מ עומד בצדו ובתוכו:"]
[" ויש אומרים דארבע אמות כו' הרא\"ש ורי\"ו בב\"י וד\"מ ס\"ס זה תמהו על הטור שלא כ' דרך קנין זה מאחר שהרא\"ש כתב דקונה ואשתמטינהו שכתבו הטור ל' ס\"ס רמ\"ג ע\"ש וגם על הר\"ב קשה שכאן כ' דין זה בל' י\"א ולקמן סימן רמ\"ג סכ\"ב כתב המחבר כך בפשיטות:"]
[" דד' אמות של אדם קונין כו' וכתב ב\"י שכ' הר\"ן ותלמידי רשב\"א וא\"ת א\"כ למה הוצרכו חכמים לתקן משיכה ומסירה בסימט' יקנה בד' אמות י\"ל דלא אמרו ד\"א אלא כשעומד ונתנו לו בתוך ד' אמותיו הא אם קדם כלי לא לפי שמקומו של כלי קנוי הוא לבעל הכלי ע\"כ ונ\"ל דוקא במתנה ומכר מחלק הר\"ן ות\"ר בכך אבל במציאה אין חילוק כדמוכח בש\"ס פ\"ק דמציעא דף י' סוף ע\"א ומ\"מ כ\"ש הוא מתנה ממציאה גבי נתנו לו בתוך ד' אמותיו ודוק וכתב עוד ב\"י שמדברי הרא\"ש נראה שאין חילוק בין קדם הוא לכלי ולעולם קנה ומביאו הד\"מ וכ' שגם מדברי ר' ירוחם נראה כן ומביאו הסמ\"ע ס\"ק ג' וכ' מדסתם הרב בהג\"ה משמע דלא חילק ודוק עכ\"ל ונראה לתרץ לדעתם הא דהוצרכו למשיכה בסימטא היינו חוץ לד' אמות כגון שמושכו בחבל א\"נ דע\"י משיכה הוי קנין דאורייתא וקנין ד' אמות אינו אלא מדרבנן:"]
siftei_kohen.en:
And so it appears proper to rule, etc. It appears that the Rama followed the Rosh in the first chapter of Bava Metzia. The Rosh writes that the Rif omitted Rav Pappa's distinction between a found object and a gift, implying that he treats them alike and follows the first resolution, namely that Rabban Gamliel transferred the movable property by agav. The Rosh nevertheless preferred Rav Pappa because he was later and because Rav Ashi answered the challenge from divorce to gift. In my opinion, however, the Rif and Rambam are primary. The entire anonymous discussion in Kiddushin 27a supports them. The Gemara seeks to prove from Rabban Gamliel's act that movable property transferred by agav must be piled upon the land, and rejects the proof only because he may have acted so as not to burden the recipients. It later asks whether land may be sold while movable property is given as a gift, and proves it from Rabban Gamliel's declaration that the tithe he would measure was given to Rabbi Yehoshua and its place rented to him. If Rav Pappa's explanation were accepted, this would prove nothing, because the acquisition could have been through the recipient's courtyard rather than agav. It is also difficult why Rabban Gamliel needed agav at all if Rav Pappa's courtyard principle itself acquired for the recipient. Although strained answers can be offered, the plain sugya excludes Rav Pappa's resolution. The Maggid Mishneh states that some rule like Rav Pappa, but the Ramban inferred from the Rif that gift is equated with finding and that the end of the first chapter of Kiddushin proves this, which is also the Rambam's view. The Ritva likewise explains that although some follow Rav Pappa because he is later, the Rif requires the recipient to stand beside the field even for a gift. The Gemara in Kiddushin treats Rabban Gamliel's act as agav, not as Rav Pappa's courtyard acquisition, and therefore Rav Pappa's resolution is not accepted. Tosafot Rid, the Semag, Rabbeinu Yerucham, and apparently the Ran agree. The Rosh's point that Rav Ashi answers for Rav Pappa is not decisive, because even if Rav Ashi held that view, the anonymous Gemara in Kiddushin does not. Moreover, the Ran explains that Rav Ashi's answer was needed even according to the accepted law, so that divorce should not present a difficulty, and the Ritva says the same. Nevertheless, since the Baal HaItur, Rabbi Yehuda bar Reuven of Barcelona, the Rosh, Raavan, the Hagahot Mordechai, and Hagahot Maimoniyot support Rav Pappa, I am not fit to decide conclusively and the matter remains a monetary doubt. But to instruct initially as the Rama does is certainly difficult, for the majority of poskim follow the Rif and Rambam, and that view appears primary.
However, if the seller, etc. The Rama's words are surprising. He derived them from the Beit Yosef in the name of Hagahot Mordechai, yet Hagahot Mordechai itself states in the name of Ri that this applies only according to the Gemara's first answer, which requires a protected courtyard even for sale or gift. Where the buyer's produce is intermixed with the owner's and no separation exists, the courtyard is unprotected. That is the Mechaber's view. According to the Rama, however, who rules like Rav Pappa that another person's intent to transfer is different, the buyer acquires even when the produce is mixed. Hagahot Mordechai states this explicitly, as do Hagahot Maimoniyot and Tosafot at the end of Bava Metzia 11a. Thus the Rama's ruling is inconsistent with his own position.
Specifically within it, etc. The wording of the Maggid Mishneh is: he stands beside it and within it.
"And thou shalt say, 'This is what is Caesar's, and that it is not like 'a path of this property', because it is written in its words, and that it is written in the column that it is not as 'a way' and that it is also difficult for them to do so
For a person's four cubits acquire for him, etc. The Beit Yosef cites the Ran and students of the Rashba: if so, why did the Sages institute pulling or delivery in an alley, since four cubits should acquire? They answer that four cubits were said only where the recipient is standing there and the object is placed within his four cubits. If the utensil was there first, the rule does not apply, because the utensil's place is already acquired to its owner. In my view, this distinction applies to gift and sale, but not to a found object, as is evident in Bava Metzia 10a. A gift is certainly no weaker than a found object when it is placed within his four cubits. The Beit Yosef further writes that the Rosh appears not to distinguish whether the person or utensil came first, and the Darkei Moshe says the same of Rabbeinu Yerucham. The Sema infers from the Rama's unqualified wording that he likewise makes no distinction. According to them, pulling was required in an alley only outside the buyer's four cubits, such as when he draws the object by a rope, or because pulling is a Torah acquisition whereas four cubits acquire only by rabbinic enactment.

turei_zahav.he: (סעיף א' בהג"ה מיהו אם המוכר כו') הג"ה זו צ"ע דבהגהת מרדכי פ"ק דב"מ כ' וז"ל אם מקנה אדם לחבירו פירות שהם בביתו ומשכיר לו מקומו ואין הפסק בין אותן הפירות לפירות ב"ה לא קנס ומקרי המצר שאינה משתמרת ובמציא' לא קנה חצר שאינה משתמרת מיהו במתנה מסיק רב פפא דזכי משום דדעת אחרת מקנה כו' ולא בעינן חצר משתמרת ואע"ג שאינו עומד בצדה עכ"ל ודברי' אלו צ"ע ליישבן ונ"ל דהא דאמר מיהו במתנ' כו' חזר ממ"ש תחלה דמתחלה היה ס"ל מכר ומציאה שוין ממילא ה"ה מתנ' דודאי אין שום חילו' בין מכר למתנה ואח"כ מחלק בין מכר למתנה ומציאה וחזר ממ"ש תחלה שהם שוין אלא דהיאך שיהי' אנו רואי' שפסק כרב פפא דבדעת אחרת מקנה קנה במתנה ומכר אפי' בכך דאין הפסק דהא עליה קאי והוא משתמר לדעת המוכר דהא לא השכיר לו רק מקום הפירות ואף שהרמ"א כתב חצר עצמו כוונתו ג"כ כן דהא מזה למד דין זה ותו דאי השכיר לו כל החצר הוה משתמ' לדעת הלוקח וכ"ה בהדיא בתוס' פ"ק דב"מ דף י"א דזה מיירי דמשתמר לדעת המוכר ע"ש בד"ה וכי בצד כו' ועוד פסק רמ"א עצמו בזה דבמוכר אמרי' דעת אחרת מקנה אותן ואמאי כ' כאן דבמעורבי' לא קנה:
turei_zahav.en: (Seif 1, in the gloss: however, if the seller, etc.) This gloss requires study. Hagahot Mordechai at the beginning of Bava Metzia writes: if a person transfers produce in his house to another and rents him the place where the produce is located, while there is no separation between that produce and the owner's own produce, the purchaser does not acquire, because the courtyard is not guarded for him. In the case of a found object, an unguarded courtyard does not acquire. However, concerning a gift, Rav Pappa concludes that the recipient acquires because another person's intent transfers it to him, and a guarded courtyard is unnecessary even when he is not standing beside it. These words themselves require explanation. It appears that the statement regarding a gift retracts the opening statement. At first the author equated a sale and a found object, and naturally a gift would have been the same. He later distinguishes a sale or gift where another person intentionally transfers ownership from a found object, thereby retracting the initial equation. In any event, we see that he rules like Rav Pappa that where another person's intent transfers ownership, acquisition works with a gift and a sale even where the produce is mixed, because the area is guarded according to the seller's awareness. The seller rented only the specific place of the produce. Although the Rama says "the courtyard itself," his intention must be the same, because this is the source from which he derived the law. If the entire courtyard had been rented, it would be guarded for the purchaser. Tosafos at the beginning of Bava Metzia 11 explicitly explains that the case concerns a courtyard guarded according to the seller. Moreover, the Rama himself rules that in a sale we apply the principle that another person's intent transfers ownership. Why, then, does he write here that when the produce is mixed the purchaser does not acquire?

mechaber.he: היו ברשות המוכר או ברשות אדם אחר שהם מופקדים אצלו לא קנה הלוקח עד שיגביה המטלטלין או עד שימשכם כמו שנתבאר: הגה מיהו אם שכר המקום שמונח בו או נתנו לו במתנה ובקנין או אפי' בדבור בעלמא קנאו דהשתא הוי ברשותו וקונה לו והא דמהני דבור בעלמא היינו ברשות אחר אבל אם מונח ברשות המוכר ואומר יזכה חצרי ללוקח במקח שקנה ממני לא קנה עד שישכיר לו מקומו ויקנה לו בא' מדרכי הקנייה (טור בשם הרא"ש ור' ירוחם נ"י ח"ב) ואם היו הפירות מופקדים ביד אחר לא סגי שיאמר תקנה חצרי ללוקח עד שיאמר כן מדעת המוכר (ב"י בשם הרמב"ן והמגיד פ"ד דמכירה):
mechaber.en:
It was in the possession of the seller or the other person who was entrusted to him that he had not given him a gift or an epitographer in his possession, and that he was given to him, and that he was given to him, and that he was given to him
The hand of the sale:

baer_hetev.he:
שימשכם. (תימא דהא משיכ' לא קנה בזה כמ"ש כל הפוסקים וברמב"ם עצמו כתב עד שיגביה הפירות או עד שיוציאם מרשותו בשכירו' מקום כו' ובדוחק י"ל דהאי עד שימשכם ר"ל יוציאם מרשותו ונלע"ד שיש ט"ס וצ"ל כמ"ש ברמב"ם. ט"ז):
קנאו. דאם היה בידו וא"ל זכה לפלוני זכה לו לפי שזכין לאדם וחצרו נמי זוכה לו כ"כ הרמב"ן וכת' ב"י נ"ל דלאו למימרא שצריך שיאמר לו זכה לפלוני אלא כיון שא"ל פירות שברשותך תנם לפלוני וקבל עליו ליתן לו קנה הלוקח דה"ל כאומר זכה בהן לפלוני עכ"ל ולי נראה דוקא שיאמר זכה לפלוני דאל"כ לא הוי תן כזכי כיון שאינו מוסרם עתה לידו אלא שכבר היו מופקדים אצלו כמ"ש בסי' קכ"ה ס"ז ע"ש וכן מוכח להדיא בחדושי הרמב"ן שם ובהרא"ש ספ"ק דגיטין ר"ס י"ז ע"ש. ש"ך:
המוכר. הטעם כת' הרא"ש שאין אדם יכול לקנות בשל עצמו לחבירו שלא ע"י אחרים אלא צריך שיגביהנו או ישכיר את מקומו בכסף או בשטר וחזקה משא"כ כשהוא בחצר אחר די"ל בעל החצר יזכה חצירי לפלוני במקח שקנה מפלוני דחצירו כידו והרי הוא יכול לזכות לחבירו בשל אחרים ע"כ. סמ"ע:
baer_hetev.en:
Until he pulls them. This is difficult, because meshichah does not effect acquisition in this case, as all the poskim state. Rambam himself writes: until he lifts the produce or removes it from the seller's domain by renting the place. With difficulty one might say that "until he pulls them" means until he removes them from the seller's domain. In my view there is a scribal error and the text should read as Rambam states. Taz.
Keno. He was given to him, and he was given to him, and he was given to him, and he was given to him. “Third:
The seller. The taste of the Rashi that no man can buy because of himself for his own affection that is not by others, but he must return his place in money or in a barrage, and he is stronger than he is in another court, the owner of the court will receive arrows to the bottom of a platoon which he has bought from the bottom of his hand, and that he can be offended by others. There, in the baraita.

beur_hagra.he:
היו ברשות כו'. לשון הרמב"ם וכגי' הרי"ף שגריס ברשות המופקדין אצלו לא קנה עד שיגביהנה או עד שיוציאנה מרשותו:
מיהו אם כו'. מתני' שם אם היה פקח כו' וכמ"ש בגמ' שם ה"ק ואם ברשות בעלים כו' וכן בפ"ה דמ"ש ופ"א דקדושין ושם בברייתא לפי גי' שלנו ברשות הלה המופקדים כו':
או נתנו כו' ובקנין. אבל בשכירות לא מהני קנין וצריך בכסף וכמ"ש תוס' בב"מ י"א ד"ה ומקומו כו' ובקדושין כז א' ד"ה ומקומו כו' כמש"ל סי' קצח ס"ט:
או אפי' כו' והא כו'. שם עד שיקבל עליו כו' אבל ברשות המוכר א"א לזכות ע"י עצמו כמ"ש בעירובין ופסחים וגטין ונדרים וב"מ ולהכי לא ערבינהו רשות מוכר ורשות המופקדין ועבתוס' שם ד"ה ארבע:
שישכיר כו' ויקנה כו'. ר"ל שהשכירות נקנה בו כנ"ל וכמ"ש ונתקבלו זה כו':
ואם היו כו'. רשב"ם ד"ה עד שיקבל כו' דהא מדין זכייה הוא שמוכר מזכה:
beur_hagra.en:
If they were in the domain of, etc. This is the Rambam’s wording, following the Rif’s reading: if they are in the domain of the custodian, the buyer does not acquire until he lifts them or removes them from that domain.
Nevertheless, if, etc. The Mishnah there says, “If he was clever, etc.,” and the Gemara explains: if it is in the owner’s domain, etc. Likewise in Maaser Sheni chapter 5 and Kiddushin chapter 1. The baraisa there, according to our reading, states “in the domain of the person with whom they are deposited, etc.”
Or he gave him, etc., and by kinyan. Rental, however, is not acquired through a kinyan sudar and requires money, as Tosafos writes in Bava Metzia 11a, s.v. “and its place,” and Kiddushin 27a, s.v. “and its place.” See above siman 198 seif 9.
Or even, etc., and that, etc. There: “until he accepts upon himself, etc.” But in the seller’s own domain he cannot acquire for the buyer through himself, as appears in Eruvin, Pesachim, Gittin, Nedarim, and Bava Metzia. For this reason the law separates the seller’s domain from the custodian’s domain. See Tosafos there, s.v. “four.”
That he should rent, etc., and acquire, etc. Meaning that the rental itself is acquired by the act described above, as stated, “and these were received, etc.”
And if they were, etc. Rashbam, s.v. “until he accepts, etc.,” because this operates through the law of conferring a benefit, whereby the seller causes the buyer to acquire.

chatam_sofer.he: שם הגה סעי' ח' יש חולקין נ"ב ע' ש"ך יד סי' קלב ס"ק כ"ה ומה שהקשה מל"מ פ"ד ממכירה הל' ה' ועיין בתשובתי ח"ס חו"מ סי' צ"ט:
chatam_sofer.en: Ibid., gloss to seif 8, "some disagree." Note: see Shach, Yoreh Deah, siman 132, seif katan 25, and what the Mishneh LaMelech asks in Hilchot Mechirah 4:5. See my Responsa Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat, siman 99.

haggahot_imrei_barukh.he: (נה"מ ח') בד"ה ולפי זה קשה כו'. נ"ב לק"מ כי ברש"י שם מפורש להדיא בזה"ל שנתן כליו באויר וקבל גלגלים לתוכו עכ"ל. הרי דוקא כשהכלי באויר וליכא מציאת זכות להמשכי' רק מצד אויר חצירו בכה"ג הוי אויר.
haggahot_imrei_barukh.en: (Netivot HaMishpat, seif katan 8) s.v. 'According to this it is difficult,' etc. Note: There is no difficulty at all, for Rashi there states explicitly: 'He placed his vessel in the air and received the disks into it.' Thus it is specifically where the vessel is suspended in the air and there is no possibility of acquisition except through the airspace of his courtyard that the airspace is effective.

kessef_hakodashim.he: בסי' ד משמע שלקנין חצר אצ"ל קנה כדגבי קנין חזקה וצלע"ע היטב. ועכ"פ מוכר שאמר הכלים מהסחורה תן עבורם סך כך ואמר הלוקח אחזירם לך ואח"כ נתיקרו הכלים ורוצה הלוקח לשלם סך שאמר המוכר והמוכר חוזר בו הרי היתה משיכה בפניו וא"צ בזה קנה בשום קנין. וגם שבשעת משיכה לא הי' דעת הלוקח לקנות מ"מ אין דבריו מחליטים שישיבם גם כשיוקרו וא"א להוציא וצלע"ע היטב: מי שקנה סחורה והיא ביד המוכר גם שנקנית בקנין מ"מ כשאומר אח"כ שתוחזר להמוכר נקנית לו ע"י חצרו המשתמרת לו בדיבור בעלמא והו"ל כמשך לפניו ואצ"ל קני בחצר ואולי מ"מ אינו כמשך בפני' כיון שעומדים בריחוק מקום מהחצר וכ"ש אם הם בעיר אחרת. ואם נתן ממון עי"ז למוכר בדרך פשר כיון שקיבל המוכר ממון י"ל דל"ש עי"ז שתיקה דלא חש להשיבו רק י"ל דשתיקה כהודאה אם לא גילה המוכר דעתו שמקבל הממון מטעם אחר: מי שהחזיר סחורה שקנה להמוכר ואחר שהי' בבית המוכר א"ל בריחוק מקום שהחזיר לו והשיב אחזיר לך מעות שנתת צל"ע כעת אם על ידי זה יש קנין חצרו של מוכר גם אם היא משתמרת לדעתו כיון שלא נאמר בזה לשון קנין ממש ואולי דכוונה שבעת שחוזר המעות יקנה וצלע"ע היטב: שותפים בסחורה שאמרו אחר כך שתוחלט לאחד והייתה אז הסחורה בעגלות ששכרו בשותפות אין דיבור מועיל שגם אם שכירות קונה על ידי דדעת אחרת מקנה וכליו קונים בסמטא כמו חצר ושכירות העגלות נקנה על ידי סטומתא הנהגה מכל מקום הרי כלים של שותפות אין א' קונה בהם משותפו. ואם הוא מנהיג העגלה י"ל שנכלל ממילא קנין שכירות העגלה להשותף על ידי משיכה בבעלי חיים להעגלה וממילא נקנה לו גם הסחורה גם דדרכה בהגבהה דוקא והו"ל כעין חצרו ומתנתו כאחד שבש"ך ז"ל סי' ר"ב וכשנכרי מוליך העגלה ואין מי מהשותפים בצד העגלה אולי לא עדיף כלי מחצר שאינו קונה רק כשמשומר לדעתו ושמירה על ידי נכרי אולי אינו מועיל גם אם משומר לדעתו על ידי בני ביתו קטנים מועיל גם שאינו שליחות מכל מקום בני ביתו טפילים לו מה שאין כן נכרי שמשמר אולי אינו מועיל וצלע"ע כעת:
kessef_hakodashim.en:
